📖 Worked example — is it AI? Four systems classified

WORKED EXAMPLE — draw the line
• A calculator computing 37 × 52 → NOT AI: fixed algorithm, no learning or adaptation.
• A spam filter that improves as you mark messages → AI (machine learning: behavior learned from data).
• A chess engine searching future moves with an evaluation function → AI (search + heuristics, no learning required — symbolic AI counts!).
• A voice assistant parsing “set a timer for 10 minutes” → AI (NLP + intent recognition).
Working definition: systems performing tasks that typically require human intelligence — perception, reasoning, learning, decision-making. The Turing test frames one benchmark: indistinguishable conversation.
⚠️ AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DEEP LEARNING
All deep learning is ML; all ML is AI; but AI includes non-learning approaches (rules, search). Options equating AI with ML are the standard distractor.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Before diving into algorithms, models, and applications, you need a working definition of AI that survives contact with reality. The popular meanings have drifted over decades; the technical meaning has too. Knowing the boundaries of the term — what it includes, what it excludes, what it has meant historically — keeps you from talking past colleagues and prevents 'is that really AI?' arguments from hijacking real discussions.

Core concepts

1. The four classic definitions. AI has been defined as: thinking humanly (cognitive modeling), thinking rationally (logic-based), acting humanly (Turing test), acting rationally (rational agents). Russell and Norvig's textbook framing. Most modern practical AI focuses on 'acting rationally' — building agents that take actions to achieve goals based on percepts.

2. The rational agent view. An agent perceives an environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators. A rational agent picks actions that maximize expected performance given its knowledge. This framing covers everything from a chess engine to a self-driving car to a chatbot. Agnostic about whether the agent thinks like a human.

3. AI as a moving target. Tasks once considered AI — playing chess, recognizing handwritten digits, search engines — become 'just software' once they work reliably. The phrase 'AI effect' captures this: AI is whatever hasn't been done yet. Today's AI is large language models, autonomous driving, protein folding; in ten years, those may just be 'tools.'

4. AI vs machine learning vs deep learning. AI is the broad field of building intelligent agents. Machine learning is one approach within AI: learning patterns from data rather than hand-coding rules. Deep learning is a subset of ML using multi-layer neural networks. Most modern 'AI' you hear about is deep learning; the field of AI is broader than that subset.

5. What AI is NOT (yet). Despite hype, current AI is narrow. It excels at specific tasks and fails outside the trained distribution. It has no understanding, intent, or consciousness in any rigorous sense. It can produce outputs that look intelligent without being so. Treating LLM outputs as authoritative reasoning is a category error.

6. Symbolic vs statistical/connectionist approaches. The historical split: symbolic AI uses explicit rules and logic ('Good Old-Fashioned AI'). Statistical/connectionist AI learns patterns from data. The latter has dominated since 2012; symbolic methods still appear in hybrid systems, planners, and reasoning engines. The pendulum has swung between them across decades.

7. Why definitions matter for engineers. When you build something with AI labels, what you're really building shapes what tests apply, what failure modes to expect, what users will assume. A symbolic expert system fails very differently from a deep learning model. Calling both 'AI' obscures the engineering specifics that matter.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Conflating AI with machine learning with deep learning — they nest; they aren't synonyms.
  • Treating LLM output as reasoning when it's pattern completion that often resembles reasoning.
  • Being defensive about whether something 'is really AI' — the field's term has moved many times and will again.
  • Assuming today's AI capabilities will generalize because they're impressive — narrowness is the rule, not the exception.

Quick recap

AI is the broad field of building rational agents that perceive and act to achieve goals. Machine learning is one approach within AI; deep learning is a subset of ML. The 'AI effect' shifts what counts as AI as techniques mature. Symbolic and statistical approaches have alternated in dominance. Current AI is narrow; treating it as broadly intelligent is a category error.

Glossary

Artificial Intelligence
Field of building agents that perceive, reason, and act to achieve goals.
Rational agent
An entity that selects actions to maximize expected performance given its knowledge.
AI effect
Tendency to redefine AI as 'whatever hasn't been done yet' once a problem is solved.
Symbolic AI
Approach using explicit rules, logic, and structured representations.
Connectionist AI
Approach using neural networks and learned weights; foundation of deep learning.
📊 FIGURE — what sits under the AI umbrella
🎯 EXAM TIP
When asked to name the subfields of AI, the expected list is ML, NLP, computer vision, robotics and planning. Machine learning is a subfield of AI, not a synonym for it — that containment is itself a common exam question.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — the history as cause and effect

WORKED EXAMPLE — why each era rose and fell
• 1950s birth: Turing’s test (1950), Dartmouth workshop (1956) names “artificial intelligence.”
• Early symbolic optimism → AI winters (70s, late 80s): promises outran compute and data; funding collapsed — the causal lesson: hype cycles follow capability gaps.
• 1997: Deep Blue beats Kasparov — brute-force search + heuristics conquer chess.
• 2012: AlexNet wins ImageNet — deep learning era begins, powered by the trio: big data + GPUs + better algorithms.
• 2016 AlphaGo (reinforcement learning); 2017 transformers; 2020s LLMs/generative AI.
Exam questions pair the milestone with its significance — memorize event → why it mattered, not just dates.
⚠️ THE WINTERS HAVE A MORAL
“What caused AI winters?” → expectations exceeding capability, then funding cuts. The modern relevance question (“could it happen again?”) expects that same mechanism.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Modern AI seems sudden — ChatGPT, autonomous driving, AlphaFold all in a few years. The history shows otherwise: 70 years of cycles, with periods of breakthrough followed by 'AI winters' of disillusion. Knowing the cycle prevents you from treating current excitement as unprecedented and helps explain why some old ideas suddenly work.

Core concepts

1. The Dartmouth conference (1956). The founding moment of the field. McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester, Shannon convene a summer workshop and coin 'artificial intelligence.' The optimism was vast: machines that could solve any problem within a generation. The term and the field begin here.

2. Symbolic era and early successes (1950s-1970s). Logic Theorist (Newell, Simon) proves theorems. ELIZA (Weizenbaum) imitates a therapist via pattern matching. SHRDLU (Winograd) understands a blocks world. Game-playing programs improve. Hopes for general intelligence are extrapolated from these narrow successes.

3. The first AI winter (mid 1970s-early 1980s). Funders realize the early systems don't generalize. Knowledge representation problems prove hard. Computer power is insufficient for ambitious approaches. UK Lighthill report (1973) is devastating to UK funding. ARPA pulls back. The field contracts.

4. Expert systems era (1980s). Narrow systems encoding human expert knowledge as rules: MYCIN (medical diagnosis), XCON (computer configuration). Briefly viable as products. Maintenance and brittleness problems eventually undermine the boom; second AI winter follows in late 1980s.

5. The statistical revolution (1990s-2000s). Machine learning rises. Bayesian networks. Support vector machines. Hidden Markov models in speech. Statistical NLP supplants symbolic. The field professionalizes — fewer grand claims, more measured progress on benchmarks.

6. The deep learning explosion (2012-present). AlexNet wins ImageNet 2012 by a wide margin using deep convolutional networks. The combination of GPUs, large datasets, and stochastic gradient descent unlocks problems thought intractable. Speech recognition, computer vision, machine translation, and game playing all see step-function improvements.

7. The transformer and LLM era (2017-present). Attention Is All You Need (2017) introduces the transformer. BERT, GPT, T5 follow. ChatGPT (2022) brings general-purpose LLMs to public consciousness. Scale — more parameters, more data, more compute — continues to surface emergent capabilities. We are still inside this wave.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Assuming current AI progress is unprecedented — the field has had multiple breakthroughs and setbacks.
  • Treating expert systems as outdated curiosities — domain-specific symbolic systems still ship in many industries.
  • Believing AI history is a steady upward line — winters are real and may recur.
  • Confusing what's hyped with what works — both expert systems and deep learning had their over-promised periods.

Quick recap

AI began as a confident research program in 1956. Symbolic AI dominated through the 1970s, suffered a winter, recovered as expert systems, suffered another winter, then was supplanted by statistical machine learning in the 1990s-2000s. Deep learning's 2012 breakthrough triggered the current wave, extended by transformers and large language models since 2017. The pattern: hype, breakthrough, plateau, repeat.

Glossary

Dartmouth conference
1956 workshop founding the AI field and coining the term.
AI winter
Periods of reduced funding and interest after over-promised breakthroughs failed to deliver.
Expert system
Rule-based AI encoding domain expert knowledge for narrow problem-solving.
AlexNet
2012 deep convolutional network whose ImageNet win launched the deep learning era.
Transformer
2017 neural architecture using attention; basis of modern LLMs.

Milestone moments: IBM Watson won Jeopardy! in 2011, beating champions at open-domain question answering. AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in 2016 — defeating a top Go player a decade before experts predicted it possible. And the pace of AI development is accelerating rapidly — capabilities that took decades now iterate in months.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — narrow vs general vs super, classified

WORKED EXAMPLE — where does each system sit?
• A chess engine that cannot drive, chat, or fold laundry → Narrow (weak) AI: superhuman in ONE domain, useless outside it.
• ChatGPT-style LLMs → still narrow (broad-LOOKING, but no genuine cross-domain understanding/agency) — a favorite trick question.
• A hypothetical system matching humans across ALL cognitive tasks → General AI (AGI) — does not yet exist.
• Intelligence surpassing the best humans in every field → Superintelligence — speculative.
EVERY deployed AI system today is narrow. The reactive → limited-memory → theory-of-mind → self-aware ladder is the other classification the exam uses (deployed systems are reactive or limited-memory).
⚠️ IMPRESSIVE ≠ GENERAL
Fluency across many topics is not general intelligence — LLMs remain narrow AI. Marking an existing product as AGI is the designed wrong answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Public discussion conflates very different ideas. Today's deployed AI is narrow — exquisite at specific tasks, useless outside them. General AI (AGI) and superintelligence are speculative. Knowing the distinctions prevents you from over-claiming for current systems and clarifies what risks and opportunities are real now versus hypothetical.

Core concepts

1. Narrow AI (ANI) — what we actually have. AI optimized for specific tasks. Image classifiers, language models, recommender systems, game players, autonomous vehicles. Each is narrow even when impressive. A chess engine doesn't translate languages; an LLM can't drive a car. Every deployed AI today is narrow, regardless of marketing.

2. General AI (AGI) — the goal. AI matching human cognitive abilities across the full range of tasks: reasoning, planning, learning, creativity, understanding. AGI is a research goal, not a product. Whether it's 5 years away, 50, or never depends on who you ask. No system today is AGI by any rigorous definition.

3. Superintelligence (ASI). AI substantially exceeding human cognitive capacity across the full range of tasks. Speculative. Whether it's reachable, what its trajectory would look like, and what implications it has are open questions debated by researchers, philosophers, and policy makers. Bostrom's 2014 book is foundational.

4. Reactive vs limited memory vs theory of mind vs self-aware. Another taxonomy: Reactive (responds to inputs without memory) — Deep Blue. Limited memory (uses past observations briefly) — most modern ML. Theory of mind (models others' beliefs) — research goal, not deployed. Self-aware (introspective) — speculative. Different framing, same insight: today's systems are early on the spectrum.

5. Why narrow AI is enough to matter. Even narrow AI has produced massive economic and social impact: search, recommendations, translation, image recognition. The narrowness doesn't prevent transformation; the breadth of applications does. Useful narrow AI is more important than speculative AGI for engineering practice today.

6. Capabilities vs generality. An LLM can write essays, debug code, summarize documents — across many domains. Is that general? Critics say no: it does language manipulation that mimics multi-domain capability without understanding. Defenders say capabilities are emerging. The terminology gets fuzzy at the frontier; expect ongoing definitional debates.

7. What this means for engineers. Build for narrow AI's strengths and weaknesses. Pick the right model for the task. Test outside the training distribution. Plan for failure modes specific to learned systems. Treat AGI claims with skepticism; treat narrow AI capabilities as already disruptive.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Claiming a narrow system 'understands' or 'thinks' — it imitates outputs, not cognition.
  • Assuming progress in one narrow domain implies progress toward AGI.
  • Designing applications as if AI is general when it's brittle outside its training distribution.
  • Dismissing narrow AI as 'not real AI' — the impact is real regardless of how you label it.

Quick recap

Narrow AI does specific tasks well; it's all we have. AGI matches human cognitive range; it's a research goal. Superintelligence exceeds human cognition; it's speculative. Categorizing systems prevents claims that outrun capabilities. Narrow AI is sufficient to be transformative; AGI debates can wait while engineers build with what works today.

Glossary

Narrow AI (ANI)
AI optimized for specific tasks; the only kind currently deployed.
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)
Hypothetical AI matching human cognitive ability across all domains.
Artificial Superintelligence (ASI)
Hypothetical AI substantially exceeding human cognition.
Reactive AI
AI that responds to current inputs without memory of past states.
Theory of mind
Capacity to model others' mental states; research goal for AI.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — a rule-based system, run by hand

WORKED EXAMPLE — a tiny medical expert system
R1: IF fever AND cough        THEN flu-likely
R2: IF flu-likely AND fatigue  THEN recommend-rest
Facts: fever, cough, fatigue
Forward chaining (data → conclusions): R1 fires (fever+cough) → adds flu-likely; now R2 fires → recommend-rest. Backward chaining (goal → support): to prove recommend-rest, need flu-likely + fatigue; to prove flu-likely, need fever + cough — all facts present ✓.
This is symbolic/GOFAI: knowledge as explicit rules, reasoning as logical inference. Strengths: explainable, precise. Weakness: brittle — someone must write every rule, and the world outruns the rulebook (the knowledge-acquisition bottleneck that ML solves by learning from data).
⚠️ FORWARD = FROM FACTS; BACKWARD = FROM GOAL
“Starts with data and derives conclusions” → forward chaining. “Starts with a hypothesis and seeks supporting facts” → backward. The direction is the exam question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Before deep learning, AI was symbolic: explicit rules, logic, structured knowledge. The approach defined the field for decades and still ships in production — expert systems, theorem provers, planners, knowledge graphs. Knowing how symbolic AI works is essential for understanding where ML doesn't fit and why hybrid systems often beat either alone.

Core concepts

1. The symbolic premise. Intelligence comes from manipulating symbols according to rules. Symbols stand for things — objects, properties, relations. Rules say what follows from what. Reasoning is logical inference. The approach mirrors how humans articulate explicit knowledge — laws, mathematics, regulations.

2. If-then rules and rule engines. The simplest symbolic system: a knowledge base of rules ('if A and B, then C') plus a working memory of facts. The engine matches rules against facts and fires those whose conditions hold, producing new facts. Forward chaining (data-driven) and backward chaining (goal-driven) are the two strategies.

3. Expert systems in practice. Medical diagnosis (MYCIN), computer configuration (XCON), tax preparation, fault diagnosis. Domain experts articulate knowledge; engineers encode it as rules. Worked best in narrow, well-bounded domains with stable knowledge. Maintenance — keeping rules consistent as knowledge evolved — proved hard.

4. Logic programming. Prolog encodes facts and rules in first-order logic; the language IS the inference engine. Querying triggers backward-chaining proof search. Niche but powerful for problems naturally expressed as logical relationships — natural language parsing, scheduling, theorem proving.

5. Knowledge representation challenges. How do you encode 'reasonable inference' or common sense? CYC (1984-present) tried explicitly: hand-coded millions of facts. Effective in narrow domains; never produced human-level common sense. The 'frame problem' (what doesn't change after an action) remains stubbornly hard for purely symbolic systems.

6. Why symbolic AI declined. Knowledge acquisition bottleneck: getting expertise out of experts and into rules is slow and brittle. Doesn't generalize: rules covering every edge case grows unmanageable. Doesn't learn: every change requires manual update. Statistical methods proved better at perception, language, and pattern recognition where rules can't be enumerated.

7. Where symbolic AI still shines. Domains with formal rules (compliance, accounting, scheduling). Domains requiring explanation (legal, medical reasoning). Domains where training data is insufficient. Hybrid neuro-symbolic systems combine learned perception with symbolic reasoning, especially for problems requiring both pattern recognition and structured logic.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Choosing rules-based AI for problems with too much variability to enumerate — brittleness sets in fast.
  • Maintaining rule bases without versioning — 'inconsistent rules' is a nightmare to debug.
  • Dismissing symbolic AI because deep learning is fashionable — many production systems still use rules where rules fit.
  • Building expert systems without ongoing expert involvement — knowledge drifts and the system becomes wrong without anyone noticing.

Quick recap

Symbolic AI manipulates symbols via explicit rules. If-then rule engines, logic programming, and knowledge representation are its core tools. It dominated AI through the 1980s and powered expert systems. Knowledge acquisition and brittleness limit it for general problems but it remains valuable in formal, well-bounded domains and as the reasoning component of hybrid systems.

Glossary

Symbolic AI
Approach using explicit rules and structured representations.
Expert system
Symbolic AI encoding domain expert knowledge as rules.
Forward chaining
Inference strategy starting from facts and applying rules to derive new facts.
Backward chaining
Inference strategy starting from a goal and working backward to known facts.
Knowledge acquisition bottleneck
Difficulty extracting human expertise into machine-usable rules.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — the three learning paradigms, one dataset each

WORKED EXAMPLE — classify the learning setup
• 10,000 emails LABELED spam/not-spam; learn to label new ones → supervised (classification; predicting a price instead → regression).
• 10,000 customer records, NO labels; find natural groupings → unsupervised (clustering; also dimensionality reduction).
• An agent plays a game, receiving rewards/penalties per move, learns a strategy → reinforcement learning (agent, environment, actions, rewards).
The tell is the DATA: labels → supervised; no labels → unsupervised; rewards from interaction → RL. Then the workflow: split data, train on the training set, evaluate on held-out test data — never grade on the data you trained on.
⚠️ OVERFITTING IN ONE SENTENCE
A model that memorizes training data (perfect train accuracy, poor test accuracy) has overfit — the reason held-out evaluation exists. This vocabulary anchors half the ML questions.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Machine learning replaced 'write rules to handle data' with 'learn rules from data.' For perception, language, prediction, and recommendation, this is overwhelmingly the right approach. Understanding the basic categories — supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement — and the typical workflow gives you the framework to evaluate any ML system you encounter.

Core concepts

1. The core idea. Don't program the rules; provide data and let the algorithm learn the rules. A learning algorithm finds parameters of a model that minimize prediction error on training data, hoping the same parameters generalize to new data. The shift from 'expressing knowledge' to 'compressing data' is the conceptual leap.

2. Supervised learning. Labeled data: each example has an input and a known correct output. Algorithm learns the mapping. Classification (spam vs not spam, dog vs cat) and regression (predict price, predict temperature). Most production ML is supervised — and most of the work is creating reliable labels.

3. Unsupervised learning. No labels. Find structure in data: clustering (group similar items), dimensionality reduction (compress while preserving structure), density estimation. Used for exploration, segmentation, anomaly detection. Often precedes supervised learning by surfacing interesting patterns.

4. Reinforcement learning. An agent acts in an environment, receives rewards, and learns a policy that maximizes cumulative reward. Game playing (AlphaGo), robotics, recommendation, RLHF for language models. Powerful when reward signals exist; scaling and stability remain research challenges.

5. Train, validate, test — the discipline. Split data into training (fit the model), validation (tune hyperparameters), and test (final evaluation, used once). Without separation, you measure how well the model memorized — useless for predicting new data. The discipline prevents fooling yourself.

6. Overfitting and underfitting. Underfitting: model too simple for the pattern. Underperforms on training and test. Overfitting: model memorizes training data instead of learning the underlying pattern. High training accuracy, poor test accuracy. Regularization, more data, simpler models, and better validation prevent overfitting.

7. The learning workflow. Define the problem and metric. Gather and clean data. Choose features (or let the model learn them). Split data. Train candidate models. Validate. Tune. Test. Deploy. Monitor for drift. The loop continues — production ML is mostly maintenance, not initial training.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Skipping the validation/test split — measuring training accuracy and calling it generalization.
  • Tuning hyperparameters on test data — leaks test info into training; overfit by another name.
  • Using ML where rules would do — sometimes a regex is better than a model.
  • Deploying without monitoring drift — training and production distributions diverge over time.

Quick recap

Machine learning learns rules from data instead of encoding them by hand. Supervised learning predicts labels from examples. Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels. Reinforcement learning optimizes actions for reward. Train/validate/test separation prevents self-deception. Overfitting versus underfitting is the central modeling tension. Production ML is mostly maintenance.

Glossary

Supervised learning
Learning a function from labeled input-output examples.
Unsupervised learning
Learning structure from unlabeled data.
Reinforcement learning
Learning a policy that maximizes cumulative reward via environment interaction.
Overfitting
Model captures training noise rather than underlying pattern; poor test performance.
Train/validation/test split
Discipline of partitioning data to prevent measuring memorization as generalization.

Training vs inference: training fits the model to data; inference is using the trained model on new data to make predictions. A decision tree is a rule-based classifier — a cascade of if-then splits on features. A random forest is an ensemble of many decision trees whose votes are combined — trading interpretability for accuracy and robustness.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — one neuron computes, one network learns

WORKED EXAMPLE — forward pass by hand
A neuron with inputs x = [1, 2], weights w = [0.5, −0.3], bias 0.2:
weighted sum = 1(0.5) + 2(−0.3) + 0.2 = 0.5 − 0.6 + 0.2 = 0.1 → activation (ReLU): max(0, 0.1) = 0.1 — the neuron “fires” weakly.
Stack neurons in layers (input → hidden → output) and you get a network; “deep” = many hidden layers. Training: compare output to the label (loss), then backpropagation nudges every weight downhill (gradient descent), thousands of times, until predictions fit. The learned weights ARE the knowledge.
⚠️ WEIGHTS LEARN; ARCHITECTURE IS CHOSEN
Training adjusts weights/biases via backprop — it does not add layers. And why deep learning now? Data + GPU compute + algorithmic advances — the same trio from the history section.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Deep learning is the form of machine learning behind most modern AI breakthroughs. Image recognition, speech, translation, language models, protein folding — all built on neural networks at scale. Understanding the basic mechanics — neurons, layers, gradients, training — explains why they work, where they fail, and what scaling actually means.

Core concepts

1. The artificial neuron. Inspired by biological neurons but only loosely. An artificial neuron takes weighted inputs, sums them, adds a bias, and passes the result through a nonlinear activation function. A scalar output. Simple math; the magic happens at scale.

2. Networks: layers and depth. Stack neurons into layers; layers feed each other. Input layer, hidden layers, output layer. 'Deep' networks have many hidden layers — sometimes hundreds. Each layer transforms the representation; later layers compose features into higher-level concepts.

3. Activation functions. Nonlinearity is essential — without it, stacking layers is equivalent to one linear transformation. ReLU (max(0, x)) is the modern default — simple, fast, works. Sigmoid and tanh are historical; softmax for classification outputs. Choice matters less than depth and data.

4. Forward pass and loss. Input flows through the network producing an output. A loss function measures distance from the correct output: cross-entropy for classification, mean squared error for regression. Loss quantifies how wrong the network is on this batch.

5. Backpropagation and gradient descent. Compute the gradient of loss with respect to each weight using the chain rule (backpropagation). Adjust weights in the direction that reduces loss (gradient descent). Repeat over millions of batches. The algorithmic core of all deep learning training.

6. Architectures matter. Generic feedforward networks work but rarely best. Convolutional networks (CNNs) for images — exploit spatial locality. Recurrent networks (RNNs, LSTMs) for sequences — exploit temporal structure. Transformers for sequences with attention — current dominant architecture for language and increasingly for vision. Architecture encodes inductive biases.

7. Why deep learning works (mostly). Neural networks are universal function approximators in theory. In practice, depth + data + compute is what unlocks them. The 2012 AlexNet result demonstrated this. Bigger models, more data, more compute keep working — sometimes called the 'bitter lesson' (Sutton): general methods that scale beat specialized methods that don't.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating deep learning as a magic universal solution — it works for some problems beautifully, fails on others.
  • Choosing architecture without understanding the inductive bias — using a generic MLP where a CNN would be far better.
  • Training without validation — billions of parameters memorize easily.
  • Ignoring compute and data costs — scale isn't free; training a frontier model costs millions of dollars.

Quick recap

Neural networks compose layers of simple weighted-sum + nonlinearity neurons. Backpropagation computes gradients; gradient descent updates weights to reduce loss. Architectures (CNNs, RNNs, transformers) encode useful inductive biases for different data types. Scale of depth + data + compute drives modern capabilities. Universal approximation in theory; engineering discipline in practice.

Glossary

Neural network
Composed layers of artificial neurons trained by gradient descent.
Activation function
Nonlinearity applied at each neuron (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh).
Backpropagation
Algorithm computing gradients of loss with respect to all weights via chain rule.
Convolutional network (CNN)
Architecture using shared weight filters; effective for grid-like data such as images.
Transformer
Attention-based architecture dominant in NLP and increasingly other domains.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Before reasoning can happen, knowledge has to be in a form a machine can manipulate. The choice of representation shapes what's easy to express, what's easy to infer, and what's missed. From propositional logic to knowledge graphs to embeddings, each representation makes some questions tractable and others impossible.

Core concepts

1. The representation question. How do you encode facts about the world? 'Birds fly' — propositional? logical? a probability? a graph? a vector? Each representation supports different operations. Choose by what you need to do, not by what's elegant.

2. Propositional logic. Atomic propositions (P, Q, R) combined with logical connectives (and, or, not, implies). Each proposition is true or false. Foundation of digital logic and Boolean reasoning. Limited: can't express 'all birds fly' or 'this bird flies' compactly. Necessary but insufficient for most real reasoning.

3. First-order logic (predicate logic). Adds variables, quantifiers (∀ for all, ∃ exists), predicates (Bird(x), Flies(x)), and functions. Can express 'all birds fly' as ∀x (Bird(x) → Flies(x)). Vastly more expressive than propositional logic. Inference is more complex; decidability becomes an issue.

4. Semantic networks and frames. Graph-based representations. Nodes are concepts; edges are relations. Frames bundle a concept with its attributes ('Bird: has-feathers, can-fly, lays-eggs'). Intuitive for humans; easier than logic to author by hand. Still used in product knowledge bases and ontologies.

5. Ontologies and knowledge graphs. Formal ontologies (OWL, RDF) give classes, properties, and axioms in standardized form. Knowledge graphs (Google's, Wikidata, Wolfram Alpha) connect entities at internet scale. Power product features like search, question answering, recommendations.

6. Embeddings — learned representations. Each entity becomes a dense vector in high-dimensional space. Similar entities have similar vectors. Word2vec, BERT, image embeddings. Don't represent meaning explicitly; capture it through proximity. The dominant representation for ML systems but harder to interpret or audit.

7. Hybrid neuro-symbolic representations. Use embeddings for perception/similarity and structured representations for explicit reasoning. Active research area: combining the strengths of learned and symbolic representations. Practical examples: retrieval-augmented LLMs, models that emit structured intermediate plans.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forcing real-world facts into propositional logic — works for textbook examples, breaks immediately on real domains.
  • Hand-building ontologies without ongoing maintenance — knowledge drifts, ontologies don't.
  • Treating embeddings as if they capture meaning explicitly — they capture statistical similarity, not semantic truth.
  • Choosing representation by elegance rather than by what operations you need to perform efficiently.

Quick recap

Representations choose what's easy to express and infer. Propositional logic is foundational but limited. First-order logic adds quantifiers and predicates. Semantic networks and ontologies are more intuitive and ship in product knowledge bases. Embeddings dominate ML systems by trading interpretability for utility. Hybrid systems are active research.

Glossary

Knowledge representation
How facts and concepts are encoded for machine manipulation.
Propositional logic
Logic of atomic true/false propositions and connectives.
First-order logic
Logic adding variables, quantifiers, predicates, and functions.
Knowledge graph
Graph-structured representation of entities and their relationships.
Embedding
Dense vector representation learned to preserve similarity in high-dimensional space.

Knowledge-representation standards: RDF (Resource Description Framework) expresses facts as subject–predicate–object triples. OWL (Web Ontology Language) defines rich ontologies — classes, properties, and constraints — on top of RDF. And rules are IF–THEN statements: IF the patient has a fever AND a rash, THEN consider X — the backbone of expert systems.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — BFS, DFS, and A*, one map

WORKED EXAMPLE — route-finding compared
Cities A→goal G with weighted roads.
• BFS explores level by level → fewest EDGES path; guaranteed shortest only when all steps cost the same; memory-hungry.
• DFS dives deep one branch at a time → low memory, no optimality guarantee, can wander.
• A* expands the node minimizing f(n) = g(n) + h(n) — cost-so-far plus a heuristic estimate to the goal (straight-line distance). With an admissible heuristic (never overestimates), A* is optimal AND efficient — the exam’s star.
Greedy best-first (h only) is fast but suboptimal; uniform-cost (g only) is Dijkstra.
⚠️ ADMISSIBLE = NEVER OVERESTIMATES
A*’s optimality guarantee lives or dies on the heuristic never exceeding true remaining cost. “What makes A* optimal?” → admissible (consistent) heuristic — the single most-tested fact.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Many AI problems reduce to search: find a sequence of moves to win the game, find the shortest path, find a configuration that satisfies constraints. The classical search algorithms — BFS, DFS, A*, alpha-beta — appear constantly in AI systems and remain the right tools for many problems even in the deep learning era.

Core concepts

1. Problem formulation. Define states, an initial state, actions (state transitions), a goal test, and a cost function. Once a problem is in this form, search algorithms can attack it generically. Most of the work is finding the right formulation.

2. Uninformed search: BFS and DFS. Breadth-First Search expands the shallowest unexpanded node first. Complete and optimal (for uniform-cost steps). Memory-heavy. Depth-First Search expands the deepest first. Memory-light, may not terminate. Iterative Deepening combines their virtues.

3. Informed search: A*. Use a heuristic h(n) estimating distance from node n to goal. f(n) = g(n) + h(n) where g is the cost from start. A* expands lowest-f-cost nodes first. Optimal if h is admissible (never overestimates). Workhorse of pathfinding, planning, and game AI.

4. Heuristic design. A* is only as good as its heuristic. Manhattan distance for grid pathfinding. Straight-line distance for routing. Domain-specific heuristics for puzzles. Better heuristic = fewer nodes expanded. Most production search optimizes the heuristic.

5. Adversarial search and minimax. Game playing involves opponents who optimize against you. Minimax: assume the opponent picks the move that's worst for you. Recursively explore alternating moves. Computationally explosive on large games.

6. Alpha-beta pruning. Optimization for minimax. Stop exploring a branch once you know the opponent will steer away from it. Can dramatically cut tree size without changing the result. Foundation of strong chess programs through Deep Blue era.

7. Modern search and Monte Carlo Tree Search. MCTS uses random simulations to estimate node value, balancing exploration and exploitation. AlphaGo combined MCTS with deep neural networks; AlphaZero learned heuristics from self-play alone. Search remains essential even in neural-heavy systems.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Choosing BFS for memory-constrained problems — exponential frontier kills you.
  • Designing inadmissible heuristics for A* — gives suboptimal solutions silently.
  • Forgetting to check for cycles — DFS without cycle detection runs forever in graph problems.
  • Treating game AI as pure neural-network play — search-and-evaluate hybrids consistently outperform pure-NN approaches at strong play.

Quick recap

Many AI problems reduce to search. Uninformed (BFS, DFS) is simple and complete but expensive. Informed (A*) uses heuristics to prune. Adversarial search (minimax with alpha-beta) handles game opponents. MCTS adds simulation-based estimation. Heuristic quality is the lever that makes search tractable on real problems. Search and learning combine in modern systems like AlphaZero.

Glossary

Search problem
Formulation of states, actions, goal test, and cost function.
Breadth-First Search (BFS)
Search expanding shallowest nodes first; complete but memory-heavy.
A* search
Best-first search using f(n) = g(n) + h(n); optimal with admissible heuristic.
Heuristic
Function estimating distance from a state to the goal; quality drives search efficiency.
Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)
Search using random simulations to estimate node value; foundation of AlphaGo.

📖 Worked example — representing knowledge, then reasoning over it

WORKED EXAMPLE — from facts to an inferred conclusion
Represent: Fido IS-A dog; dogs ARE mammals; mammals ARE warm-blooded (a semantic network / ontology of IS-A links).
Reason: follow the chain → Fido is warm-blooded — a fact NEVER stated, derived by inheritance over the hierarchy. In logic form: dog(Fido), ∀x dog(x)→mammal(x), ∀x mammal(x)→warmblooded(x) ⊢ warmblooded(Fido) — deduction (sound); induction generalizes from examples (probable); abduction guesses the best explanation (diagnosis).
Knowledge representation = HOW facts are stored (rules, frames, networks, logic); reasoning = deriving what follows. Both together make an inference engine.
⚠️ DEDUCTION vs INDUCTION vs ABDUCTION
Certain-from-rules → deduction. Pattern-from-examples → induction (ML’s engine). Best-explanation-from-effect → abduction. Three words, three exam questions.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Knowledge is what you have stored; reasoning is what you do with it. The two are entangled in practice but distinct in principle. AI systems that excel at one often fail at the other — large language models have vast knowledge but inconsistent reasoning; logic-based systems reason precisely but know little. Understanding the distinction helps diagnose what's going wrong when an AI system gets things wrong.

Core concepts

1. Two faculties, separately measured. Knowledge: facts you can recall and reference. Reasoning: deriving conclusions from facts according to rules. Different cognitive operations even in humans. Test the two separately when evaluating AI: 'what is X?' (knowledge) vs 'given X and Y, what follows?' (reasoning).

2. Deductive reasoning. From general rules to specific conclusions. 'All humans are mortal. Socrates is human. Therefore Socrates is mortal.' Truth-preserving — if premises are true, conclusion must be. The bedrock of formal logic and mathematics. Computationally well-understood.

3. Inductive reasoning. From specific examples to general patterns. 'Every swan I've seen is white, so all swans are white.' Not truth-preserving — exceptions exist. The basis of scientific generalization and machine learning. Powerful but provisional.

4. Abductive reasoning. Inference to the best explanation. 'The grass is wet; it probably rained.' Not deductively valid (sprinkler could have run), but rational. How humans diagnose, debug, and explain. Hard for AI to do well; LLMs sometimes mimic it but often produce unsupported confidence.

5. Common-sense reasoning. What everyone knows but no one writes down. 'You can't push a rope. Glass breaks if you drop it. Strangers shouldn't enter houses.' Decades of attempts (CYC) hand-coded common sense; LLMs absorb much of it from text. Still a frontier — current AI fails common-sense tests humans pass without thinking.

6. Reasoning under uncertainty. Real-world knowledge isn't binary; conclusions aren't certain. Bayesian reasoning updates beliefs as evidence comes in. Probabilistic graphical models encode dependencies. Modern AI typically combines learned probabilistic representations with calibration to handle uncertainty.

7. The reasoning gap in modern LLMs. LLMs have impressive knowledge breadth but uneven reasoning. They can solve some logic problems and fail at near-identical variants. Chain-of-thought prompting helps; it's not a fix. The gap between 'knows things' and 'reasons reliably' is a current research frontier and a practical engineering concern.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating an LLM's confident output as reasoning when it might be pattern matching to similar-looking inputs.
  • Relying on deduction in domains where premises are uncertain — conclusions inherit the uncertainty.
  • Conflating 'knows facts' with 'understands relationships' — different capabilities, different evaluations.
  • Using AI for reasoning-critical decisions without human verification of the reasoning chain.

Quick recap

Knowledge stores facts; reasoning derives conclusions. Deductive reasoning is truth-preserving. Inductive generalizes from examples. Abductive infers explanations. Common-sense reasoning is everyone's tacit knowledge. Modern AI mixes vast knowledge with uneven reasoning — especially LLMs, where confidence often outruns reliability. Engineer accordingly.

Glossary

Knowledge
Stored facts a system can recall.
Reasoning
Process of deriving new conclusions from existing facts and rules.
Deduction
Truth-preserving inference from general rules to specific conclusions.
Induction
Generalization from specific examples to broader patterns.
Abduction
Inference to the best explanation given observations.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Reading and writing AI code requires recognizing patterns that recur across implementations: data pipelines, model definition, training loops, evaluation, inference. The vocabulary is large but the structure is consistent. Once you can recognize the pieces, you can navigate any AI codebase.

Core concepts

1. The data pipeline. Load data. Clean it. Transform it (tokenize, normalize, augment). Batch it. Iterate over it during training. Most ML code is data plumbing, not model code. Tools: PyTorch DataLoader, TensorFlow tf.data, pandas. Bugs here often look like model bugs.

2. Model definition. Specify the architecture: layers, connections, activations. In PyTorch: define a class extending nn.Module with forward(). In TensorFlow/Keras: stack layers in Sequential or use the functional API. The structural blueprint; doesn't yet have learned weights.

3. The training loop. For each epoch: for each batch: forward pass to predictions, compute loss, backward pass to gradients, optimizer step to update weights. Repeat. Logging, checkpointing, early stopping wrap around it. Identical structure across PyTorch projects.

4. Loss functions and optimizers. Cross-entropy for classification, MSE for regression, custom for special cases. Optimizers: SGD, Adam, AdamW. Hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, weight decay) tune the dynamics. Often the difference between 'works' and 'doesn't' is hyperparameter choice, not architecture.

5. Evaluation and metrics. Run model on held-out data; compute metrics. Classification: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC. Regression: MSE, MAE, R². Generation: BLEU, ROUGE, perplexity. Choose metrics that match the actual goal — accuracy on imbalanced data is misleading.

6. Inference and serving. Production code that runs the trained model on new inputs. Often radically different from training code: optimized for latency and throughput, not flexibility. Quantization, distillation, ONNX export, TensorRT. The line between research code and production code is wide.

7. Reading AI code top-down. Find the data pipeline (where data loads). Find the model definition (the architecture). Find the training loop (where loss is computed and weights are updated). Find evaluation (where metrics are reported). Once you orient on these four, the rest is configuration and instrumentation.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Spending hours debugging model code when the bug is in the data pipeline.
  • Logging only loss without per-class metrics — masks systematic bias.
  • Optimizing the wrong metric — high accuracy on imbalanced data misses what matters.
  • Treating training code as production code — they have very different requirements and idioms.

Quick recap

AI code structure: data pipeline, model definition, training loop (forward → loss → backward → optimizer step), evaluation, inference. Most projects are data plumbing wrapped around a small model definition. Loss functions and optimizers tune the dynamics. Production inference is a separate concern from training. Recognizing these pieces lets you navigate any codebase.

Glossary

Data pipeline
Code that loads, transforms, batches, and feeds data to a model.
Training loop
Iterative process: forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimizer step.
Loss function
Quantifies prediction error; gradient of loss drives weight updates.
Optimizer
Algorithm updating model weights using gradients (SGD, Adam, etc.).
Inference
Running a trained model on new inputs to produce predictions.

📘 Deep dive: the Python data stack

Python is popular for data work because of its readable syntax plus a mature ecosystem. NumPy provides fast numerical computing over N-dimensional arrays (vectorized math instead of Python loops). pandas provides the DataFrame — tabular data manipulation: filtering, grouping, joining, cleaning. Matplotlib/Seaborn visualize. The standard flow: load into a DataFrame → clean → analyze with vectorized operations → visualize → report.

Beyond the basics: scikit-learn is the classical machine-learning library (regression, trees, clustering); TensorFlow/Keras provide high-level neural-network APIs; CUDA is NVIDIA’s GPU programming platform that accelerates training.

📊 FIGURE — where models actually run, and who keeps them running
🎯 EXAM TIP
MLOps is DevOps for machine learning — the same automation and reliability discipline, extended to cover the things software alone does not have: training data, model versions, and the fact that a deployed model degrades as the world drifts away from its training set.

📖 Worked example — match the algorithm to the problem

WORKED EXAMPLE — five problems, five algorithms
• Predict house price from size/location → linear regression (continuous output).
• Spam or not, with a probability → logistic regression / naive Bayes (fast text baseline).
• Human-readable IF-THEN decisions for loan approval → decision tree (explainable; many trees = random forest for accuracy).
• Group customers with no labels → k-means clustering (choose k centroids, assign, recompute, repeat).
• Classify a new point by its neighbors → k-NN (lazy learner: no training, distance vote at query time).
The mapping skill — output type + data type + explainability need → algorithm — IS the exam.
⚠️ REGRESSION OUTPUTS NUMBERS, CLASSIFICATION OUTPUTS CLASSES
“Logistic regression” is a CLASSIFIER despite its name — the most reliable trick option in this section.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A few dozen algorithms cover most production AI systems. Knowing what each does, what data it expects, and what its strengths are lets you pick the right one — or at least recognize what the team is using and why. The newest algorithms get attention; the older ones still ship the most products.

Core concepts

1. Linear and logistic regression. Linear: predict a continuous output as weighted sum of inputs. Logistic: predict a class probability via sigmoid. Cheap, interpretable, often a baseline. If a fancy model can't beat well-tuned logistic regression, the data — not the model — is the problem.

2. Decision trees and random forests. Decision tree: recursive splits on features. Interpretable but prone to overfit. Random forest: ensemble of trees trained on resampled data. Robust, handles mixed data types, often best general-purpose tabular ML. Gradient boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM) take this further.

3. k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN). No training: store the data. Predict by finding k closest points and voting / averaging. Simple, surprisingly effective baseline. Slow at inference; sensitive to feature scaling and dimensionality.

4. Support Vector Machines (SVM). Find the hyperplane maximizing margin between classes. Kernel trick handles non-linear boundaries. Workhorse of pre-deep-learning ML for classification. Less common today but still appears in text classification and small-data settings.

5. k-Means clustering. Unsupervised: partition data into k clusters by minimizing within-cluster variance. Iterative, sensitive to initialization. Pre-step for many pipelines (segmentation, vector quantization, exploration). Variants (k-medoids, mini-batch k-means) for specific needs.

6. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Deep learning for images. Filters slide over the image extracting features at each position. Pooling reduces resolution. Stacks of conv layers learn hierarchical features. ResNet, EfficientNet, ViT. Dominant in computer vision until ViTs arrived; both ship in production.

7. Transformers and attention. Attention computes weighted sums of all positions, letting each position attend to all others. Stacked transformer blocks dominate modern NLP. BERT for understanding, GPT for generation, T5 for sequence-to-sequence. Increasingly used in vision (ViT) and other domains too.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Using a deep model when logistic regression or gradient boosting wins on small tabular data.
  • kNN on high-dimensional data — distances become meaningless (curse of dimensionality).
  • k-Means on data without spherical clusters — results are misleading.
  • Reaching for transformers for everything — many problems don't have enough data to train them well from scratch.

Quick recap

Linear/logistic regression for baselines. Decision trees and random forests for tabular data. kNN as a simple non-parametric baseline. SVMs for some classification settings. k-Means for clustering. CNNs for images. Transformers for sequences. Most production systems pick a small subset and tune well rather than chase the newest architecture.

Glossary

Logistic regression
Linear model with sigmoid output for binary classification.
Random forest
Ensemble of decision trees trained on bootstrap samples; reduces overfitting.
k-Nearest Neighbors
Non-parametric algorithm classifying by majority vote of k closest training points.
k-Means
Iterative clustering algorithm partitioning data into k groups.
Attention
Mechanism letting each position weight contributions from all other positions.
📊 FIGURE — PCA in one screen
🎯 EXAM TIP
PCA is Principal Component Analysis, a dimensionality-reduction technique that re-expresses the data on new axes ordered by how much variance each explains. It is unsupervised — it never looks at the labels, which is what separates it from a supervised feature-selection method.

📖 Worked example — choosing the algorithmic approach

WORKED EXAMPLE — one scheduling problem, three attacks
Assign 30 exams to time slots without student conflicts:
• Exhaustive search — try everything: correct but combinatorially explosive (slots^30).
• Heuristic/greedy — order exams by most-conflicts-first, assign each the first legal slot: fast, usually good, no optimality guarantee.
• Optimization/metaheuristics — hill climbing from a random schedule, swapping pairs to reduce conflicts; genetic algorithms breed good schedules; simulated annealing escapes local optima by sometimes accepting worse moves.
The trade triangle: guarantees vs speed vs generality. Constraint-satisfaction framing (variables, domains, constraints) + backtracking is the structured middle path.
⚠️ HEURISTICS TRADE OPTIMALITY FOR SPEED
“Fast, good-enough, no guarantee” is the heuristic signature; “escapes local optima via randomness” is simulated annealing/GA. Match the phrase to the approach.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Beyond specific algorithms, certain methodological approaches recur. Greedy strategies, dynamic programming, divide-and-conquer, randomized methods, evolutionary algorithms — each is a problem-solving pattern that informs algorithm design. Recognizing the approach behind a solution helps you adapt it to new problems.

Core concepts

1. Greedy algorithms. Make the locally best choice at each step. Fast and simple. Sometimes globally optimal (Dijkstra, Kruskal, Huffman), sometimes a useful heuristic. Test on examples before assuming optimality. The cheapest approach worth trying first.

2. Dynamic programming. Break a problem into overlapping subproblems; cache results to avoid recomputation. Foundation of many AI algorithms — Bellman equation in RL, sequence alignment, parsing, longest common subsequence. The key skill: recognize when subproblems repeat.

3. Divide and conquer. Split the problem into independent pieces, solve each, combine. Mergesort, FFT, parallel computation. Works when subproblems are roughly independent. Less universal than dynamic programming but cleaner when it applies.

4. Randomized algorithms. Use randomness deliberately. Randomized quicksort. Monte Carlo simulations. Random projections for dimensionality reduction. Often dramatically simpler or faster than deterministic equivalents. Gives probabilistic guarantees rather than worst-case ones.

5. Heuristics and approximation. Many problems are NP-hard — no known polynomial algorithm finds the optimum. Heuristics give 'good enough' solutions fast. Approximation algorithms give guaranteed bounds (within 2x optimal, etc.). Most production AI on hard problems uses heuristics.

6. Evolutionary and genetic algorithms. Maintain a population of candidate solutions. Select better ones, recombine and mutate, iterate. Works on problems where gradients aren't available (combinatorial, discrete). Niche but persistently useful — neural architecture search, hyperparameter optimization, robotics.

7. Composing approaches. Real systems blend approaches. AlphaGo: search (MCTS) + learning (policy and value networks) + heuristics + parallelism. Production NLP: pre-trained transformer + retrieval + reranking + post-processing rules. Approach selection isn't either/or; it's about composition.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Assuming greedy works without verifying — many natural-looking greedy solutions are subtly wrong.
  • Reaching for dynamic programming when subproblems aren't actually overlapping — adds complexity without speedup.
  • Using randomization for problems where deterministic guarantees matter (medical, financial, legal).
  • Treating evolutionary algorithms as universal optimizers — slow compared to gradient methods when gradients exist.

Quick recap

Approach matters as much as algorithm. Greedy for local choices. Dynamic programming for overlapping subproblems. Divide and conquer for independent splits. Randomization for simplicity or speed. Heuristics for hard problems. Evolutionary methods for combinatorial spaces. Real systems compose these — the engineering skill is matching approach to structure.

Glossary

Greedy algorithm
Algorithm making locally best choices at each step.
Dynamic programming
Solving overlapping subproblems by caching solutions.
Divide and conquer
Decomposing a problem into independent subproblems.
Randomized algorithm
Algorithm using randomness for simplicity, speed, or guarantee shape.
Heuristic
Approximate method providing good but not necessarily optimal solutions.
📊 FIGURE — two names that come up by acronym
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two acronyms worth knowing cold. PSO — Particle Swarm Optimization is the swarm-inspired metaheuristic where candidate solutions are drawn toward the best position found so far. VAE — Variational Autoencoder is a generative model: unlike a plain autoencoder it learns a distribution, so you can sample it to produce new data.

📖 Worked example — a vision pipeline, end to end

WORKED EXAMPLE — how the app reads a parking sign
1. Capture: the image is a grid of pixel numbers (RGB).
2. Preprocess: resize, normalize brightness.
3. Feature extraction: a CNN’s early layers detect edges → shapes → letters (learned filters, not hand-coded).
4. Tasks stack up: classification (“this is a sign”), detection (box around it), segmentation (exact pixels), OCR (read the text).
Applications: medical imaging, face recognition (+ its privacy/bias debates), autonomous driving. Failure modes worth naming: lighting/occlusion, and training-data bias (faces underrepresented → higher error rates).
⚠️ CLASSIFY vs DETECT vs SEGMENT
Whole-image label → classification. Boxes → detection. Pixel-level masks → segmentation. The exam hands you a task description and wants the right level.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Computer vision is the field that gives machines a sense of sight. From medical imaging to autonomous driving to phone cameras, deployed CV systems affect billions of users. The progression from hand-crafted features to deep learning to vision transformers is a microcosm of AI's broader trajectory.

Core concepts

1. The image as data. An image is a grid of pixels, each with intensity values (1 channel for grayscale, 3 for RGB). High-dimensional but highly structured: spatial proximity matters, edges matter, scale matters. The structure is what algorithms exploit.

2. Classical CV: hand-crafted features. Pre-deep-learning, engineers designed features: SIFT (scale-invariant points), HOG (histograms of oriented gradients), Haar features (face detection). Each captured something useful but required domain expertise. Pipelines stacked features with classical classifiers.

3. Convolutional neural networks for vision. CNNs replaced hand-crafted features with learned ones. The 2012 AlexNet result on ImageNet showed deep CNNs vastly outperformed prior methods. Subsequent architectures (VGG, ResNet, EfficientNet) refined depth and efficiency. Foundation of modern CV through the 2010s.

4. Vision tasks. Classification: what's in this image? Object detection: what's where? Bounding boxes. Semantic segmentation: classify every pixel. Instance segmentation: distinguish individual objects of the same class. Pose estimation, depth, optical flow. Each task uses similar backbones with task-specific heads.

5. Vision transformers. ViT (2020) applied transformers to vision: split image into patches, treat patches as tokens, attend across all of them. Often matches or exceeds CNNs on large-scale tasks. Hybrid CNN-ViT architectures are common; both flavors ship in production today.

6. Practical concerns. Data: huge labeled datasets are expensive (ImageNet, COCO). Annotation tools and pipelines are their own engineering. Augmentation (flips, crops, color jitter, mixup) effectively multiplies data. Pretrained models + fine-tuning is the standard starting point.

7. Real-world CV pitfalls. Training data biased toward certain demographics, lighting, contexts. Adversarial examples — small pixel perturbations — fool classifiers reliably. Domain shift: CV models trained on one camera fail on another. Production CV is mostly fighting these issues, not chasing benchmark numbers.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Training a model from scratch when pretrained weights would converge in a fraction of the time.
  • Ignoring class imbalance — the rare class always loses without correction.
  • Trusting benchmark accuracy as production-ready — domain shift will surface fast.
  • Building face recognition or similar without explicit attention to demographic bias and consent.

Quick recap

Computer vision turns pixel grids into useful interpretations: classification, detection, segmentation, pose, depth. CNNs dominated through the 2010s; vision transformers rival them today. Pretrained backbones plus fine-tuning is the standard. Production challenges are bias, adversarial robustness, and domain shift more than benchmark accuracy.

Glossary

Computer vision
Field of building systems that interpret visual data.
Convolutional layer
Network layer applying learned filters across a 2D grid.
Vision transformer (ViT)
Transformer architecture applied to image patches.
Object detection
Task of identifying and localizing objects with bounding boxes.
Semantic segmentation
Pixel-level classification of every pixel in an image.

Convolution slides a small filter across the image, detecting local patterns (edges, textures) wherever they appear. Pooling downsamples feature maps, keeping strong signals while shrinking size. Detector families: YOLO — single-pass, real-time object detection; the R-CNN family — region-based, proposing regions then classifying them: more accurate historically, slower.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — an NLP pipeline on one sentence

WORKED EXAMPLE — “The service was great, but delivery was slow.”
1. Tokenize: [the, service, was, great, …].
2. Normalize: lowercase, maybe stem/lemmatize (delivery→deliver).
3. Represent: bag-of-words counts, or embeddings — vectors where similar meanings sit near each other (king−man+woman≈queen).
4. Task: sentiment analysis → mixed (positive service, negative delivery); NER would tag entities; translation, summarization, QA are sibling tasks.
Why NLP is hard: ambiguity (“I saw her duck”), sarcasm, context. Modern engines (transformers/LLMs) learn language patterns from vast corpora rather than hand-written grammar rules.
⚠️ EMBEDDINGS = MEANING AS GEOMETRY
The exam’s favorite NLP concept: words/documents as vectors, similarity as distance. “Which representation captures semantic similarity?” → embeddings, not bag-of-words.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

NLP went from struggling at basic translation in 2010 to writing essays, debugging code, and answering complex questions today. The transformer architecture and large language models drove the revolution. Understanding how NLP systems work — and where they still fail — is essential for any engineer building anything language-touching today.

Core concepts

1. The language problem. Language is high-dimensional, structured, ambiguous, and contextual. The same sentence means different things in different contexts. Words have multiple senses. Grammar isn't strict. Decades of NLP wrestled with these properties through linguistic theory; deep learning largely sidestepped them by learning from data.

2. Tokenization and embeddings. Text becomes tokens (words, subwords, or bytes). Each token maps to a learned embedding vector. Word2Vec showed embeddings could capture surprising semantics ('king - man + woman ≈ queen'). Subword tokenization (BPE, SentencePiece) handles rare words and multilingual text.

3. From RNNs to transformers. RNNs (LSTM, GRU) processed sequences left-to-right with hidden state. Worked but struggled with long contexts and parallelization. Transformers (2017) replaced recurrence with attention — process all positions in parallel, attend across distances. Decisive shift for the field.

4. BERT vs GPT — the two flavors. BERT (encoder-only): bidirectional, designed for understanding (classification, QA, NER). GPT (decoder-only): left-to-right, designed for generation. T5 and similar are encoder-decoder for sequence-to-sequence. Each architecture suits different tasks.

5. Pre-training and fine-tuning. Pre-train on huge unlabeled text corpora with self-supervision (next-token prediction, masked language modeling). Fine-tune on small task-specific labeled data. The two-stage paradigm replaced training from scratch and made NLP work on small data volumes.

6. Large language models. Scaling pre-training to billions of parameters and trillions of tokens unlocked emergent capabilities — instruction-following, chain-of-thought reasoning, in-context learning. GPT-3, GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, Llama. Capability per parameter continues to improve.

7. Tasks LLMs do and don't do well. Do well: text generation, summarization, translation, coding assistance, question answering on knowledge present in training. Less reliable: precise reasoning, current events, math beyond simple cases, factual claims requiring verification. Hallucination — fluent confident wrong answers — is the persistent failure mode.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Trusting LLM output as fact-checked — hallucination is constant.
  • Fine-tuning when prompting would do — and prompting when fine-tuning would be more reliable.
  • Building NLP systems without testing on out-of-distribution inputs — production text is messy.
  • Treating LLMs as databases — they're language predictors with stale knowledge.

Quick recap

NLP turns text into representations and back. Tokens become embeddings. Transformers replaced recurrent networks. BERT-style models do understanding; GPT-style do generation; T5 handles sequence-to-sequence. Pre-train on massive text, fine-tune (or prompt) for tasks. LLMs at scale show emergent capabilities. Hallucination remains the central reliability concern.

Glossary

Tokenization
Splitting text into tokens (words, subwords, or bytes).
Embedding
Dense vector representing a token, learned during training.
Transformer
Attention-based architecture replacing recurrence in modern NLP.
Pre-training
Initial unsupervised training on large corpora with self-supervision.
Hallucination
LLM outputs that are fluent and confident but factually wrong.

NLP models start with pretraining on a massive text corpus (predicting words), then adapt to tasks. Core tasks: sentiment analysis — is this text positive/negative; named entity recognition (NER) — find people, places, organizations in text; and the application layer — chatbots and assistants built on all of the above.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — two ways to recommend a movie

WORKED EXAMPLE — why Netflix suggests what it does
• Collaborative filtering: users who rate like YOU liked “Inception” → recommend it. Needs no film metadata — just the ratings matrix. Weakness: cold start (new user/new item has no ratings).
• Content-based: you liked sci-fi thrillers; “Inception” IS one → recommend. Needs item features; can’t surprise you outside your profile (over-specialization).
• Hybrid: blend both — the practical answer to cold start + narrowness.
Ethics rider: engagement-optimized recommenders can create filter bubbles and amplify extreme content — the metric-vs-wellbeing divergence again.
⚠️ COLD START BELONGS TO COLLABORATIVE
“New item has no ratings — which approach struggles?” → collaborative filtering. Content-based handles new items (they have features) but struggles with new USERS’ unknown tastes.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Recommendation systems decide what billions of users see daily — products, videos, news, friends, songs. They're among the most economically consequential AI systems ever deployed. The basic algorithms are decades old; the engineering and ethical complexity at scale is enormous.

Core concepts

1. The recommendation problem. Given a user, a catalog of items, and historical interactions, predict items the user will engage with. Variants: ranking (order items), top-N selection (pick best k), exploration (introduce new items). Universally framed as optimizing engagement, sometimes with countervailing constraints.

2. Collaborative filtering. 'Users who liked X also liked Y.' Matrix factorization decomposes the user-item interaction matrix into user and item embeddings. Predict missing entries. Foundational and surprisingly effective. Doesn't require item content, just interactions.

3. Content-based filtering. Recommend items similar to ones the user liked, based on item features. Works well when item content is rich and interactions are sparse. Less prone to popularity bias, but creates filter bubbles.

4. Hybrid and deep learning approaches. Most production systems combine collaborative + content + side information (time, location, device). Two-tower neural networks learn embeddings for users and items separately, score with dot product. Sequential models (RNNs, transformers) capture session-level behavior.

5. The cold-start problem. New users and new items have no interaction history. Content-based features, demographic priors, exploration strategies (explicitly recommend new items to learn about them) address this. The problem doesn't fully go away — it's a perpetual concern, especially at the edges of the catalog.

6. Production realities. Latency budgets (under 100 ms typically). Catalogs of millions of items. Two-stage retrieval-and-ranking architectures. Online experimentation (A/B tests) drive every change. Personalization plus diversity plus business rules — rec systems carry many constraints simultaneously.

7. Engagement vs well-being. Optimizing for engagement (clicks, time spent, return rate) sometimes optimizes against user well-being. Filter bubbles, addictive feedback loops, recommendation of harmful content. The most-discussed ethical issue in modern AI sits squarely here. Some platforms add explicit objectives (diversity, quality, freshness); others don't.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Optimizing engagement metrics without considering downstream effects on users or society.
  • Cold-start ignored until users churn from a bad first experience.
  • Recommending only popular items — feedback loop amplifies existing popularity.
  • Lack of explainability — users don't trust or accept recommendations they can't make sense of.

Quick recap

Recommendation systems predict user engagement with items. Collaborative filtering uses interaction patterns; content-based uses item features; hybrids combine both. Production systems use two-stage retrieval-and-ranking with deep models. Cold-start, latency, diversity, and the engagement-vs-well-being tension are persistent challenges.

Glossary

Collaborative filtering
Recommendation based on user-item interaction patterns.
Content-based filtering
Recommendation based on item features and user preferences.
Matrix factorization
Decomposing the user-item matrix into low-rank user and item embeddings.
Cold start
Difficulty recommending for new users or items with no interaction history.
Two-stage retrieval-and-ranking
Production architecture: fast retrieval narrows candidates, slower ranking orders them.

📖 Worked example — the sense-plan-act loop

WORKED EXAMPLE — a warehouse robot fetches a box
1. Sense: lidar + cameras build a map; localize itself in it (SLAM).
2. Plan: path-search (A*!) around obstacles to aisle 7; task planner sequences: navigate → align → grasp.
3. Act: motor controllers execute; grip sensors confirm.
4. Loop continuously — a human walks by, sensors update, the plan replans.
Decision systems share the skeleton minus motors: sense (data in) → decide (rules/ML/RL) → act (recommendation/action). Autonomy levels grade how much a human stays in the loop — full autonomy in open environments remains the hard frontier (uncertainty, edge cases, safety).
⚠️ THE LOOP IS THE ANSWER SHAPE
“How does a robot/agent operate?” → sense → plan/decide → act, repeated. Naming which stage a described failure lives in (bad sensing? bad planning?) is the applied question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Robotics integrates perception, planning, and control to act in the physical world. AI decision systems — autonomous vehicles, drones, industrial automation, medical decision support — combine multiple AI techniques into systems that act, not just predict. The integration is what makes them harder than any single component.

Core concepts

1. The robotics stack. Sensing (cameras, lidar, IMUs). Perception (interpret sensor data). Localization and mapping (where am I, what's around). Planning (where to go, how). Control (motor commands). Each layer is its own discipline; integration is where systems succeed or fail.

2. Perception in robotics. More than CV. Sensor fusion combines multiple modalities (vision + lidar + radar). Tracking objects across frames. Estimating depth, motion, and pose. Real-world conditions (rain, glare, dust) test perception harder than benchmarks.

3. SLAM — Simultaneous Localization and Mapping. Robot doesn't have a map AND doesn't know where it is. Builds the map and estimates its position simultaneously. Foundational problem; classical (EKF, particle filters) and learned approaches both ship. Required for autonomous navigation in unknown environments.

4. Planning and control. Path planning: from A to B avoiding obstacles. Motion planning: feasible trajectories through joint space. Control: commands that achieve trajectories despite real-world uncertainties (friction, slip, wind). Hierarchies: high-level task planning, mid-level motion, low-level control.

5. Reinforcement learning in robotics. Promise: robots learn skills through trial and error. Reality: physical robots are slow and expensive to train; sim-to-real transfer adds complexity. Successes (dexterous manipulation, locomotion) come from massive simulation paired with careful real-world fine-tuning.

6. Decision systems beyond physical robots. AI making operational decisions: route planning, energy grid management, financial trading, medical diagnosis support. Same conceptual challenges (perceive, decide, act) without the physical actuators. Often subject to stricter regulatory and explainability requirements than consumer AI.

7. Safety in autonomy. When AI acts autonomously, failures are immediate and consequential. Verification (formal proofs of properties), validation (testing across scenarios), runtime monitors (detect anomalies and degrade safely), human oversight protocols. The discipline is older than current AI hype and ignored at peril.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Optimizing perception alone and treating planning as a follow-on — the integration is what's hard.
  • Sim-to-real assumption: 'we tested in simulation' — physical world surfaces problems sim never showed.
  • Deploying learned policies without runtime monitoring — failure modes can be sudden and catastrophic.
  • Treating safety as a final review step — safety-critical systems require it built into every stage.

Quick recap

Robotics integrates sensing, perception, localization, planning, control. SLAM solves 'where am I and what's around.' Classical and learned approaches both ship. Reinforcement learning is promising but slow on physical robots. Decision systems extend the same concerns to non-physical autonomy. Safety engineering is non-negotiable in autonomous systems.

Glossary

Sensor fusion
Combining multiple sensor modalities into unified state estimates.
SLAM
Simultaneous Localization and Mapping; building a map and locating within it concurrently.
Path planning
Computing a trajectory from start to goal avoiding obstacles.
Sim-to-real transfer
Training in simulation and deploying on physical hardware; the gap between is a known challenge.
Runtime monitor
Component that watches a system's behavior at runtime and triggers safe-degradation if needed.
